passage:
Sunday. Lalit scrolled past a headline in the hostel mess: "Coffee drinkers live longer, big study finds." He read it twice, then showed Santosh. "Bro, coffee is basically medicine."
Wednesday. Lalit was now drinking cup after cup of filter coffee and had stopped his evening run, because the coffee "was doing the work". Santosh raised an eyebrow. "Maybe coffee people just have jobs and money and friends to go to cafés with. Or maybe people who get ill stop drinking coffee."
"Nah, the study is huge," Lalit said.
The next Monday. Lalit, jittery and short on sleep, finally opened the actual article. Near the bottom: "The study shows a link; it does not show that coffee causes longer life." He sighed, put on his running shoes, and went back to his one morning cup.

qa.q: What did the line near the bottom of the article say?
qa.a: "The study shows a link; it does not show that coffee causes longer life."

qa.q: Why did the headline convince Lalit so quickly?
qa.a: It was short, confident and said 'big study', so Lalit read it as coffee making people live longer and liked the idea of an easy shortcut.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Lalit swapped his evening run for coffee because of a headline; reading the full article and seeing it showed only a link sent him back to running.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the coffee study?
qa.a: Santosh thinks something else could explain it, like coffee drinkers having money and friends, or ill people giving up coffee.

grounding: It shows a student turning a headline about coffee drinkers into the belief that coffee itself causes longer life, until hidden factors come up.

passage:
Another coffee, Ujjwal? Sit. Let Parveen aunty tell you something. When I was nineteen, in my second year at Aligarh, a magazine in the reading room said coffee drinkers live longer. I had never liked coffee, but I started drinking it with every meal. I told my roommates it was for my health. I really believed each cup was adding years to my life.
Then my statistics professor brought that same article to class. He asked us, "Who drinks coffee in this country?" People with a bit of money, office jobs, time to sit in coffee houses. People with healthier lives for many reasons. And people who are already unwell often give coffee up. The coffee wasn't the reason; it was riding along with other things. I felt so foolish. So drink your coffee because you like it, not because a headline told you to.

qa.q: Where did Parveen aunty read about coffee drinkers?
qa.a: In a magazine in the reading room, in her second year at Aligarh.

qa.q: Why did Parveen start drinking coffee with every meal though she never liked it?
qa.a: She felt hopeful that each cup was adding years to her life, so the headline turned a link into a reason to change her habits.

qa.q: What question did the professor ask, and why does it help?
qa.a: He asked who drinks coffee in the country, which brought out hidden factors like money, office jobs and free time that could explain longer lives.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal take this story from Parveen aunty?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel gently teased about the coffee, but also see that she is sharing her own mistake so he won't trust headlines too quickly.

grounding: It shows a student believing coffee caused longer life after reading a headline, before learning hidden factors can explain the link.

passage:
Twenty minutes before the inter-college debate, Shalini was still scribbling her opening line on the back of a canteen bill: "Science has proven that coffee makes you live longer." She had seen the headline that morning, "Coffee drinkers outlive non-drinkers", and it had felt like a gift.
Kavitha, her teammate, read it over her shoulder and winced. "Proven? It said coffee drinkers outlive others. That's not the same."
"It's the same thing."
"What if richer people drink more coffee and also see doctors more? Or people who fall ill stop drinking it? Then the coffee isn't doing anything."
Shalini looked at the clock. Twelve minutes. She had no time to find the study, no data pack, only the headline. She crossed out "proven" and wrote "linked", then stared at the word, unconvinced.

qa.q: What did Shalini write her opening line on?
qa.a: The back of a canteen bill.

qa.q: Why does Shalini think 'drinkers outlive non-drinkers' means the same as 'coffee makes you live longer'?
qa.a: Shalini felt pleased because the headline seemed like a gift for her debate, and when two things go together it seems natural that one causes the other, so the difference feels like nitpicking.

qa.q: What could Shalini say in the debate that stays honest?
qa.a: She could say coffee drinkers were found to live longer but that other things, like money or illness, might explain it, so the link isn't proof.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had time to read the full study?
qa.a: She might find out whether it looked at money or illness, and could build her argument on what it really showed instead of on a headline.

grounding: It shows a student under time pressure treating a coffee-and-long-life headline as proof that coffee is the cause.

passage:
Maria, twenty, was eating toast on the balcony of her Bengaluru PG when the headline popped up on her phone: "Coffee drinkers live longer, huge study finds."
By lunch she had bought a bag of filter coffee powder and a steel tumbler set. By the evening she was on her third cup.
"You hate coffee," Simran said from the doorway.
"I'm learning to like it. It's science. The study had half a million people."
"Did it say why they lived longer?"
"Because of the coffee, obviously."
Simran picked up the phone and scrolled. "It says coffee drinkers in the study also walked more and smoked less."
Maria took the phone back and scrolled up to the headline again. "Yeah, but the big number is about coffee." She poured another cup, grimacing at the bitterness.

qa.q: How many people did Maria say the study had?
qa.a: Half a million people.

qa.q: How does Maria feel about the coffee headline, and what shows it?
qa.a: Maria feels convinced and eager, buying coffee powder by lunch and drinking a third cup by evening, even grimacing at the bitterness, because the huge study sounds like proof.

qa.q: At which moment could Maria think again, and what could she ask?
qa.a: When Simran reads that coffee drinkers also walked more and smoked less; Maria could ask whether those habits, not the coffee, explain the longer lives.

qa.q: How might Simran feel watching Maria drink coffee she dislikes?
qa.a: Simran is probably amused and a little puzzled that Maria forces down a bitter drink because of a headline, especially after pointing out the other habits.

grounding: It shows a student reading that coffee drinkers live longer and believing coffee is the reason, missing hidden third factors.

passage:
"Ma, we have to switch Nani from tea to coffee."
"Why, Mahima beti? She's had tea for sixty years."
"I read it. People who drink coffee live longer. It was a big study."
Sharmila set down the pressure cooker lid. "Who drinks coffee in our family?"
"Masi's family in Chennai. And they're all healthy."
"Masi's family also walks on the beach every morning and eats early."
"That's extra. The coffee is the main thing."
"And maybe people who are already healthy keep drinking coffee, and people who fall ill stop?"
Mahima frowned. "Why would anyone stop?"
"Your Nana stopped coffee when his heart was weak. So he was in the tea group at the end."
Mahima was quiet for a moment, then: "Still. Coffee people live longer. I read it."

qa.q: What does Mahima want to switch Nani to?
qa.a: From tea to coffee.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel about switching Nani to coffee, even after Sharmila's points?
qa.a: Mahima feels confident and a little defensive, frowning and then repeating "I read it", because the headline and Masi's healthy family seem to prove it.

qa.q: What choice could Mahima make instead of changing Nani's drink?
qa.a: Mahima could look up whether the study checked things like walking and eating habits, or whether ill people stop drinking coffee, before deciding coffee is the cause.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the coffee claim?
qa.a: Sharmila sees other reasons, like morning walks and early meals, and the chance that sick people give up coffee, so to her the link doesn't prove coffee is the cause.

grounding: It shows a student believing coffee makes people live longer, while her mother points to hidden third factors and reversed direction.
